content: This is an updated Cochrane review originally published in 2017. Acute appendicitis, which refers to inflammation of the appendix, can be classified as either simple or complicated. Complicated appendicitis includes conditions such as appendiceal phlegmon and appendiceal abscess. Appendiceal phlegmon is characterized by diffuse inflammation in the lower right quadrant of the abdomen, while an appendiceal abscess is a localized collection of pus in the abdominal cavity. These conditions account for approximately 2% to 10% of all cases of acute appendicitis. Patients with appendiceal phlegmon or abscess typically require an appendicectomy to alleviate symptoms such as abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting, and to prevent complications like peritonitis, which is an infection of the abdominal lining. The timing of surgery for these conditions is a subject of ongoing debate. Surgery can be performed early, either immediately upon hospital admission or within a few days, or it can be delayed, occurring several weeks later during a subsequent hospital admission. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of early versus delayed appendicectomy on overall morbidity and mortality in patients with appendiceal phlegmon or abscess. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, as well as trial registries, on June 11, 2023. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared early and delayed appendicectomy in patients with these conditions, regardless of language, publication status, or participant age. Eight RCTs involving 828 participants were included in the analysis. These trials were conducted in the USA, India, Nepal, and Pakistan. Seven trials focused on appendiceal phlegmon, while one trial addressed appendiceal abscess. All included studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias due to issues such as lack of blinding, absence of published protocols, unclear randomization methods, and insufficient information on follow-up duration. For appendiceal phlegmon, seven trials involving 788 participants (both pediatric and adult) were analyzed. Of these, 394 participants underwent early appendicectomy (either open or laparoscopic) during the same hospital admission after the appendiceal mass resolved, while the remaining 394 participants received delayed appendicectomy following initial conservative treatment. No deaths were reported in either group. The evidence was highly uncertain regarding the impact of early appendicectomy on overall morbidity (risk ratio [RR] 0.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 2.86; 3 trials, 146 participants), wound infections (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.02; 7 trials, 788 participants), and the development of fecal fistulas (RR 1.75, 95% CI 0.36 to 8.49; 5 trials, 388 participants). However, early appendicectomy may reduce the rate of abdominal abscess formation (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.80; 4 trials, 626 participants) and shorten the total length of hospital stay by approximately two days (mean difference [MD] −2.02 days, 95% CI −3.13 to −0.91; 5 trials, 680 participants). On the other hand, early appendicectomy may increase the time away from normal activities by about five days (MD 5.00 days, 95% CI 1.52 to 8.48; 1 trial, 40 participants), but this evidence is also highly uncertain. For appendiceal abscess, one trial involving 40 pediatric participants was included. In this study, 20 participants underwent early laparoscopic appendicectomy, while the other 20 received delayed laparoscopic appendicectomy approximately 10 weeks later following initial conservative management. No deaths were reported in either group. The trial did not provide data on overall morbidity, specific complications, or time away from normal activities. The evidence was highly uncertain regarding the effect of early appendicectomy on the total length of hospital stay (MD −0.20 days, 95% CI −3.54 to 3.14). In conclusion, for patients with appendiceal phlegmon, very low-certainty evidence suggests that early appendicectomy may reduce the rate of abdominal abscess formation. However, the evidence is highly uncertain regarding its effects on overall morbidity and other complications. Early appendicectomy may also reduce the total length of hospital stay but could increase the time away from normal activities. For patients with appendiceal abscess, the available data are sparse, and it remains unclear whether early or delayed appendicectomy offers significant benefits or harms. Further research is urgently needed to address these uncertainties. Future trials should establish standardized criteria for the use of antibiotics, percutaneous drainage of abscesses prior to surgery, and the resolution of appendiceal phlegmon or abscess. Additionally, outcomes such as time away from normal activities and length of hospital stay should be consistently reported.
